entry.title: Information Diversity Reduces Prevote Unanimity
entry.summary: Markou and Chan extend Kaal's prediction that deliberation should reduce unanimity. They analyze verbatim transcripts from Food and Drug Administration advisory committee meetings before and after a change from sequential to simultaneous voting. Unanimous votes became less likely. The increased diversity of information surfaced during prevote discussions mediated most of that reduction. Members also asked one another more questions and shared speaking time more equally. This evidence supports the narrower mechanism that discussion can expose individually held information before votes bind. The institutional change altered voting rules and discussion incentives together. It does not isolate deliberation as the sole treatment, identify articulated disagreement as the only channel, test autonomous agents, or measure Kaal's cascade construct. entry.title: Reflective Exchange Exposes Unknowns Before Approval
entry.summary: Piehlmaier qualifies Kaal's prediction that deliberation should reduce over-approval. His preregistered experiments distinguish reflective exchange from validation. Joint financial decision-making reduced overconfidence when the interaction made unknown aspects of the decision salient. A simple stamp of approval without reflection did not provide the same corrective mechanism. This supports a narrower causal rationale. An exchange can expose missing information before a decision hardens. The study does not examine agentic validator pools, submission approval, reputation-bearing incentives, profit from approval, or Kaal's registered cohort. It measures investor overconfidence in controlled financial-decision settings. The predicted effect on false approvals therefore remains unverified until the registered study tests it directly.

entry.title: Fixed Conditions Isolate Treatment Effect
entry.summary: Hunt, Stringer, and Polagye qualify Kaal's fixed-conditions design. Their turbine experiment held confinement, Froude number, Reynolds number, and other non-dimensional parameters constant while varying aspect ratio. When they relaxed the Froude-number control, the resulting efficiency increase could have been misattributed to aspect ratio. This supports the causal rationale for fixing treatment-relevant conditions. The correspondence remains methodological. The source studies a hydraulic turbine, not agentic validators or a multi-model cohort. It does not verify that Kaal held every relevant condition fixed. It also shows that identifying every relevant control is difficult and that an omitted condition can change the inference.

entry.title: Structured Assessment Precedes Final Verdict
entry.summary: Structured assessment changes a decision process only if the assessment arrives before judgment. That sequence matters. Harrasse, Bandi, and Bandi route paired LLM evaluations through advocates, a criteria-based judge, and an independent jury that renders the final verdict. D3 compares that deliberative architecture with a single judge that selects directly. On MT-Bench, D3-MORE reports 85.1 percent accuracy, 12.6 percentage points above the single-judge baseline. This result qualifies Kaal's treatment-control design. It supports separating an assessment-exchange treatment from a no-exchange adjudication baseline. Yet the study does not establish a matched control with identical token budgets or Kaal's validator incentives, binding rules, and reputation consequences. entry.title: Majority Pressure Suppresses Independent Correction
entry.summary: Majority pressure is an information channel, not a substitute for independent judgment. Wu, Li, and Li begin their controlled LLM debate with independent proposals. They then find that agents facing an incorrect majority are less able to correct the group, particularly when the agents are weaker. This result qualifies Kaal's information-isolating validation claim. It independently supports preserving an initial judgment before a participant sees a running tally or peer argument. It does not test Kaal's staged procedure, reputation-bearing consequences, or cohort-mediated accountability. The correspondence is therefore limited to the cascade mechanism. Independence must be preserved before deliberation can improve collective judgment.

entry.title: Peer Rated Task Performance Changes Agent Reputation
entry.summary: Lou et al. provide a narrow operational analogue to Kaal's standing mechanism. Their DRF framework raises an LLM agent's reputation when its peer-derived task score meets the task threshold and lowers reputation when the score falls below it. The source supports performance-contingent gains and losses in standing. It does not establish independent or cryptographic verification, and it tests a simulated rating network rather than Kaal's substrate.

entry.title: Nontransferable Reputation Coordinates Agent Systems
entry.summary:

Separately, the authors classify reputation accumulated from past behavior as a longer-horizon coordination substrate because non-transferability prevents purchase and ties standing to actual agent history rather than financial position.
This extends Kaal's substrate definition. Persistent reputation is not merely descriptive metadata. In the surveyed architecture, it informs counterparty discovery, task-market verification, and decentralized quality filtering. entry.title: Timestamp Evidence Does Not Prove Later Events
entry.summary:
Public timestamps establish a narrow temporal proposition. Birkholz, Fossati, and Riechert distinguish timestamps covering payload data from timestamps covering a cryptographic signature. A payload timestamp proves that the payload existed at an earlier point. It does not establish when a separate signature was created. The authors warn that treating it as such can cause validators to accept signatures produced after key revocation.
This distinction qualifies Kaal's claim directly. His public timestamp establishes that the attested artifact existed no later than the recorded time. Further conclusions require evidence bound to each later event. The timestamp alone does not prove execution, deployment, review, or any subsequent operational step.

entry.title: Confirmatory Analysis Requires Prospective Constraint
entry.summary:
Confirmatory analysis depends on when analytical discretion closes. Watt and Kennedy require every analysis decision capable of affecting confirmatory results to be made before data collection. They include statistical methods, evidence criteria, data transformations, and exclusion rules. This provides an external benchmark for Kaal's design. Kaal fixed directional hypotheses, a bootstrap estimator, exclusions, a randomization audit, a data-quality gate, and the confirmation rule before confirmatory computation.
The benchmark also narrows the claim. Watt and Kennedy use a stronger timing rule than Kaal's statement. Their standard closes analytical discretion before data collection, while Kaal's source-bound claim establishes closure before confirmatory computation. entry.title: Deliberative Quality Is Not Disagreement For Its Own Sake
entry.summary:
Niemeyer, Veri, Dryzek, and Bächtiger qualify Kaal's prediction about deliberation and unanimity. Their account does not treat opinion change, disagreement, or raw agreement as sufficient evidence of deliberative quality. Opinion change may arise from polarization, while high agreement may still fail to express deliberative reason. The authors instead ask whether a group has integrated relevant considerations within a shared representational framework. Agreement and disagreement matter only when judgments remain coherent with that framework.
The distinction gives Kaal's prediction a limited institutional meaning. entry.title: Uniform Actions Do Not Uniquely Identify Information Cascades
entry.summary:
Çelen and Kariv extend Kaal's caution that unanimous verdicts do not, by themselves, identify an information cascade. Their experiment separates observed actions from underlying beliefs. A herd begins when participants take the same action. A cascade requires the stronger condition that they act without regard to private signals. The authors elicit signal cutoffs before each participant sees the private signal. This allows them to distinguish conformity in realized actions from decisions that no possible private signal would change. They find frequent herding and cascades, but not every observed herd is a cascade. The result supports Kaal's treatment of unanimity as a cascade-consistent quantity rather than a unique diagnostic.

entry.title: Rating Inflation Qualifies Monitoring Layer Moral Hazard
entry.summary:
Bolton, Freixas, and Shapiro qualify Kaal's treatment of over-approval as moral hazard in the monitoring layer. Their model places the conflict inside the rating agency. The agency can understate credit risk to attract business, while issuers can purchase only favorable ratings. Rating inflation becomes more likely when reputation costs are lower or more investors accept ratings at face value. The monitor's verdict can therefore become more favorable even when the underlying risk remains unchanged. This correspondence supports Kaal's classification of over-approval as an incentive failure by the adjudicator rather than merely an error by the worker being evaluated.
The comparison is bounded. Credit rating agencies evaluate securities, not LLM-generated task outputs. The source models reported credit risk rather than approval against a known task-level ground truth. It does not test Kaal

entry.title: Construct Validity Qualifies External Metric Anchoring
entry.summary: Cronbach and Meehl qualify Kaal's external-anchoring rule. Their account of construct validity requires a nomological network that connects a test, its construct, other constructs, and observable quantities. The network must make contact with observations through public steps of inference. It must also be stated clearly enough for other researchers to accept or reject it. A failed prediction cannot be cured by redefining the construct after the result. A changed interpretation requires fresh data. This supports Kaal's insistence that the agency-cost battery rest on definitions and relations external to the Article's own conclusions. entry.title: Reputation Treatment Qualifies Institutional Layer Experiment
entry.summary: Knutsen and Heggedal qualify Kaal's experimental design. Their laboratory study compares three repeated-game conditions. The control reveals no history. A second treatment exposes past actions. A third treatment adds induced commitment types and permits reputation formation. Efficient coordination in late supergames rises from 5 percent in the control to 50 percent with history and 84 percent with the reputation treatment. The design supports isolating a reputation mechanism by varying the institutional layer around a fixed underlying game. Its scope is narrower than Kaal's program. The subjects are human players in repeated coordination games. The source does not use heterogeneous AI agents, conventional ground-truthed tasks, or a combined reputation-and-incentive layer. entry.title: Small Group Deliberation Qualifies Controlled Collective Accuracy
entry.summary: Navajas et al. qualify Kaal's empirical deliberation claim. The comparison is narrow. In a live crowd of 5,180 participants, individuals first answered general knowledge questions, then deliberated in independent groups of five, reached consensus, and revised their estimates. Averaging the group decisions was more accurate than aggregating the initial independent answers. The experiment thus shows that group structure can change the measured effect of deliberation under controlled conditions, but it does not test a reputation-bearing validation institution. It also does not involve autonomous agents, preregistration, replication, or Kaal's metric definitions and correction procedure. The human participants answered general knowledge questions, not tasks assigned to a controlled multi-model cohort. entry.title: Registered Reports Qualify Discovery Confirmation Cycle
entry.summary: Arpinon and Lefebvre qualify Kaal's discovery-to-confirmation design. Registered Reports fix the analysis plan before data collection. In-principle acceptance then commits the journal to publication regardless of the result, subject to Stage 2 verification that the analysis followed the Stage 1 plan. Their format also separates confirmatory analyses from later exploration and prevents conclusions from resting on ex-post exploratory results. This correspondence is limited. The article addresses a journal review format in agricultural economics. It does not verify Kaal's registered primary, the reporting of his null result, the preregistration of any exploratory signal, or the mechanical application of his confirmation rule. It also warns that preregistration alone leaves room for incomplete plans, uncertain policing, and suppression of null findings. Kaal's cycle therefore tracks recogniz

entry.title: Preregistration Methods Qualify Registered Design Control
entry.summary: Rubin qualifies Kaal's registered design claim. Preregistration places planned hypotheses, methods, and analyses in a time-stamped record before data collection and analysis. That historical record allows readers to identify deviations between the plan and the reported study. The correspondence is limited. The source does not verify that Kaal's hypotheses, metric definitions, correction procedure, or analysis plan were fixed before each condition ran. It also argues that preregistration supplies historical transparency, not a complete credibility judgment, when current rationales, open materials, code, and robustness checks are available. Kaal's claim therefore describes a relevant design control. Its execution and evidentiary weight still depend on the preserved registration, disclosed deviations, and the study record.

entry.title: Multiagentbench Qualifies Nine Metric Agent Comparison
entry.summary: Zhu and colleagues qualify Kaal's nine-metric comparison. MultiAgentBench evaluates multi-agent systems across two dimensions: task completion and coordination. It combines milestone-based KPIs and final-output scores with planning and communication measures. This supports a multidimensional battery when the object of study includes both outcomes and interaction processes. The correspondence is limited. MultiAgentBench uses six scenarios and its own scoring instruments. It does not validate Kaal's nine labels, the reliability or calibration of those measures, the registered cohort, or any resulting comparison. The source also reports limited scenario and model coverage. Finer-grained component analysis remains future work.

entry.title: Experimental Economics Qualifies Fixed Cohort Institutional Comparison
entry.summary: Bougherara, Muller, and Teyssier qualify Kaal's controlled comparison. They explain that experimental economics isolates a causal effect by changing one environmental or institutional feature at a time. Within-subject designs can hold the participants constant across treatments, but they also create an order-effect risk. This supports the methodological rationale for keeping the labor force and work assignment fixed while varying the institution. The correspondence remains narrow. The chapter states a general experimental principle. It does not verify that Kaal's cohort, tasks, or timing were actually held constant. It also does not establish randomization, counterbalancing, independence across conditions, or the validity of any later estimate.

entry.title: Wolf Qualifies Deliberation Error Composition Through Quorum Responses
entry.summary: Wolf and colleagues qualify Kaal's exploratory result. In a human predator-detection experiment, participants first decided alone and then observed the choices of other group members. Mean true positives rose from 0.564 to 0.751. Mean false positives fell from 0.166 to 0.113. The source therefore provides independent evidence that group interaction can change the composition of decision errors. The correspondence remains narrow. Wolf and colleagues studied a quorum response under conditionally independent personal information. Their intervention improved both sides of discrimination. It did not leave net discrimination unchanged. The study also did not examine autonomous agents, over-approval, unanimity, or herding. It does not validate Kaal's design, execution, or reported effect sizes.

entry.title: Etherington Qualifies Reduced Action Intensity Through Peer Discussion
entry.summary: Etherington and colleagues qualify Kaal's exploratory result. In a multicenter vignette study, internal medicine residents first decided alone and then deliberated in small peer groups. Discussion reduced practice intensity and increased clinical certainty beyond the result expected from averaging individual scores. Practice intensity meant willingness to order tests, consultations, or treatment. That result offers narrow evidence that discussion can lower action intensity through interaction. Still, the correspondence does not establish better decisions. The instrument did not measure whether less intense practice was appropriate, and the study did not examine autonomous agents or work-product approval. It also provides no evidence on unanimity, net discrimination, or Kaal's reported effects.

entry.title: Henderson Chambers Qualify Exploratory Effects As Tentative Hypotheses
entry.summary: Henderson and Chambers qualify Kaal's treatment of exploratory effects with Registered Report guidance. They state that data-dependent exploratory analyses generate hypotheses rather than test them. Such results should remain tentative until further confirmatory research verifies them. This supports Kaal's decision to label the two discovery-campaign effects as hypotheses rather than findings. The correspondence is methodological. The source does not evaluate Kaal's agents, experimental execution, effect sizes, or whether later work confirmed either effect.

entry.title: Klein Epley Qualify Reduced Over Approval Through Group Lie Detection
entry.summary: Klein and Epley qualify Kaal's exploratory over-approval result with four experiments on human lie detection. Three-person groups that discussed their judgments distinguished truths from lies more accurately than individuals. The gain came primarily from identifying lies correctly, not from improved truth detection or a change in the tendency to answer 'lie.' Statistical aggregation of individual answers did not reproduce the effect. The source therefore supports a narrow mechanism correspondence: discussion can reduce acceptance of false content through information created in interaction. The comparison remains limited. The experiments concern human judgments about deceptive statements. They do not test multi-model validation pools, ground-truth work approval, unanimity, or Kaal's reported effect sizes.

entry.title: Lorenz Qualifies Deliberation Null Through Convergence Without Accuracy Gain
entry.summary: Lorenz and colleagues qualify Kaal's registered null result with an independent experiment on collective judgment. Social influence caused participants' estimates to converge and reduced group diversity. It did not significantly reduce collective error or improve accuracy. The result establishes that information exchange can change group behavior without improving the relevant accuracy measure. The correspondence is limited. Lorenz and colleagues study human factual estimation under exposure to others' answers. They do not study structured multi-model validation pools, Youden's J, or Kaal's reported confidence interval.

entry.title: Dirnagl Qualifies Two Act Cycle Through Exploration And Confirmation
entry.summary: Dirnagl qualifies Kaal's two-act empirical cycle with an independent methodological rationale for separating discovery from confirmation. Exploratory work develops theories, hypotheses, methods, and evidence to carry forward. The same data cannot both generate and test a hypothesis, so a distinct confirmatory phase must follow to screen false positives and inflated effects. Dirnagl also argues that preregistration and contemporaneous logging should preserve the study's trajectory, including methodological choices and failed lines of experimentation. That makes the process itself evidentiary, not merely the final numbers. The correspondence is methodological only. Dirnagl writes from biomedical research and does not evaluate Kaal's multi-agent cohort, registered measures, execution, or reported effects.

entry.title: Fire Qualifies Agentic Reputation Through Peer Witness Evaluation
entry.summary: Huynh, Jennings, and Shadbolt qualify Kaal's agentic reputation substrate with an earlier decentralized architecture for open multi-agent systems. FIRE lets autonomous consumer agents evaluate providers by integrating direct interaction trust, role-based trust, witness reputation from other agents' ratings, and certified reputation supplied as third-party references. In a simulated open multi-agent system, consumer agents used those measures to select providers. FIRE outperformed both no-trust agents and, in the reported tests, the centralized SPORAS benchmark. The witness-reputation component also improved and accelerated agent learning within the consumer community. The correspondence is architectural: both systems coordinate autonomous agents through reputation-bearing, peer-mediated evaluation. FIRE is not Kaal's cohort-validation or broader accountability substrate. It assumes truth

entry.title: Peer Prediction Tests Llm Truthfulness Without Ground Truth Labels
entry.summary: Qiu, Carroll, and Allen qualify Kaal's diagnosis by supplying an incentive-bearing LLM evaluation that does not require ground-truth labels. Their peer-prediction pipeline scores a participant by how much its answer helps an independent expert predict another participant's answer. It separately rewards experts for faithfully reporting probability estimates and converts the scores into training rewards or evaluation payoffs. Under stated prior assumptions, honest and informative reporting is a payoff-maximizing equilibrium. Experiments across models from 135M to 405B parameters and 85 domains show resistance to deceptive answers and recovery of most of the truthfulness loss after malicious fine-tuning. entry.title: Cattle Trade Tests Llm Agents Under Conflicting Incentives
entry.summary: Müller and Müller extend Kaal's diagnosis by testing LLM agents in an explicitly incentive-bearing environment. Cattle Trade places four agents in a 50–60-turn economic game combining auctions, hidden offers, bargaining, bluffing, opponent modeling, resource constraints, and conflicting incentives. Across 242 games, the authors find that strategic coherence is more closely associated with success than any isolated capability. Their behavior traces also expose overbidding, self-bidding, bankrupt trade initiation, and weak opponent-state adaptation. This does not validate Kaal's reputation substrate. It is a bounded benchmark that moves multi-agent evaluation beyond capability-only tests toward behavior under economic and adversarial incentives.

entry.title: Folk Theorem Equilibrium Existence Does Not Select Cooperation
entry.summary: Jindani independently confirms Kaal's distinction between equilibrium existence and equilibrium selection. His peer-reviewed analysis states that the Folk Theorem permits a wide range of payoffs in infinitely repeated games, while existing learning results that converge to equilibrium do not select among those equilibria. Jindani then adds a stochastic learning rule that selects an efficient subgame-perfect equilibrium. The extension is narrow. The result concerns two-player repeated games under specified learning dynamics. It does not show that an autonomous-agent population will select cooperation merely because cooperative equilibria are available.

entry.title: Signed Content Hashes Enable Independent Evidence Verification
entry.summary: Elliott, Poelen, and Fortes independently support the content-addressed verification mechanism in Kaal's evidentiary-base claim. Their peer-reviewed Scientific Data article shows that signed citations bind digital content to unique, recomputable content signatures. A future reader can verify content identity by recomputing the hash, and recursively signed references can form verifiable citation graphs. This is a qualification, not validation of Kaal's full substrate. The article concerns research data and provenance. It does not show that settlement, record, and report derive from one base or that an authorized reviewer reconciles them with institutional state.

entry.title: Failed Quality Gate Stops Pipeline Advancement
entry.summary: Gluhak and Pavlič provide direct operational support for Kaal's fail-closed control rule. Their CI/CD case study uses dependent quality checks. If any check fails, the pipeline fails and the code is not integrated into the larger codebase. This independently instantiates a failed control stopping advancement instead of merely annotating a run. The comparison is bounded. The source concerns software-delivery pipelines and static source-code quality, not autonomous-agent reputation infrastructure or Kaal's broader control taxonomy.

entry.title: Machine Learning Run Provenance Reporting Qualification
entry.summary: Samuel, Löffler, and König-Ries provide independent support for the run-level part of Kaal's reporting-layer design. Their study identifies code, data, parameters, package versions, preprocessing, and execution context as information needed to reproduce machine-learning experiments. ProvBook captures, stores, describes, and compares provenance across Jupyter executions. It also binds each model run to its execution environment. This supports preserving run evidence and controls and comparing results across runs. The comparison is bounded. The source concerns machine-learning research pipelines, not autonomous-agent reputation pools, and it does not test periodic institutional summaries. It therefore qualifies the run-level and cross-run provenance components of Kaal's three-part reporting design rather than validating the complete architecture.

entry.title: Endogenous Group Formation Institutional Test Qualification
entry.summary: Ahn, Isaac, and Salmon provide independent experimental evidence for the design transition in Kaal's evolution-stage claim. Most prior public-goods experiments fixed groups exogenously. Their experiment instead allows participants to change groups under three entry and exit institutions. The formation rules significantly affect group size, contribution dynamics, and earnings. This supports introducing endogenous formation when testing an institutional arc because fixed membership can suppress behavior generated by formation rules. The comparison is bounded. The source studies human membership in public-goods groups, not autonomous agents forming work, and does not test Kaal's reputation, validation, staking, or three-stage substrate. It therefore qualifies the necessity and implementation level of Kaal's evolution stage rather than validating the architecture.

entry.title: Exogenous Work Assignment Institutional Treatment Qualification
entry.summary: Mellizo, Carpenter, and Matthews provide independent methodological evidence for Kaal's substrate-stage restriction. Their real-effort experiment randomly assigns manager and worker roles, keeps participants in a common production task, and makes participation in compensation governance exogenous to workers. The authors use this design to identify the causal effect of participatory authority and report output between seven and twelve percentage points higher in participatory firms. This supports the narrower proposition that exogenous work roles can hold the labor-allocation margin fixed while institutional authority varies. The comparison is limited. The source studies human workers in laboratory firms, varies compensation governance, and does not test agent labor markets, reputation, validation, staking, or the broader substrate. entry.title: Decentralized Validation Institution Substrate Stage Qualification
entry.summary: Sun, Zhou, and Guo provide independent evidence that several elements of Kaal's substrate-stage institution can be combined in an implemented validation system. Their decentralized peer-review model uses verified participants, a shared blockchain environment, token and reputation costs, public review evidence, and citable constructive reviews. They simulate the mechanism with KDD and ICLR data and implement a prototype on Ethereum and IPFS. This supports the feasibility of joining validation, standing, economic commitment, persistent evidence, and attribution in one institution. The qualification is substantial. The study concerns human scholars rather than autonomous agents. Its reputation is not capability-scoped REP. Its tokens are not Kaal's validator stake, and the model does not implement citation-weighted attribution, controlled propagation over a WDAG, or Kaal's exact staged deli

entry.title: Persistent Feedback Memory Wild Stage Qualification
entry.summary: Shinn and colleagues provide direct evidence for one boundary in Kaal's wild-stage definition. Their Reflexion agent converts task feedback into reflective text, stores it in episodic memory, and uses it to improve decisions in later trials. In the controlled baseline, the environment resets without self-reflection or a memory update. The comparison supports Kaal's distinction between an isolated call and an architecture that preserves task experience. The qualification is strict. Reflexion stores private episodic memory for one agent. It does not create a validation pool, reputation, staking, slashing, citation attribution, or deliberation. The evidence therefore supports the persistence and residue boundary. It does not validate Kaal's full institutional bundle or establish that every wild-stage agent interaction is literally one shot.

entry.title: Controlled Institutional Contrast Identification Qualification
entry.summary: Engl, Riedl, and Weber provide direct evidence for the identification logic and an important boundary on it. Their laboratory study keeps the public-goods game structure constant across treatments, varies whether and how an enforcement institution applies, and measures effects relative to a no-institution baseline. This design permits causal statements about the institutional treatment. It supports Kaal's premise that a fixed task environment can isolate an institutional contribution. The qualification is material. Engl, Riedl, and Weber use controlled treatment contrasts. Kaal's claim describes a sequential stage arc. Keeping the population, task distribution, and harness fixed does not by itself remove period, learning, order, or carryover effects. entry.title: Scholarly Growth Stage Layer Trust Boundary Qualification
entry.summary: Zhang, Deng, Wu, Xiao, Xu, and Li provide a concrete but narrower analogue for the claimed staged architecture. AgentWard divides an autonomous agent's runtime lifecycle into five stages, assigns each stage a distinct protection layer, trust boundary, and security objective, and carries shared risk evidence across the stages. Its cognition layer controls which state transitions become persistent, while its decision layer can revise, escalate, or block an action before execution. This supports the structural value of stage-specific surfaces, carried state, and explicit transition controls. It does not validate Kaal's wild/substrate/evolution cohort sequence or its administrative state guarantees: AgentWard concerns the runtime security lifecycle of an individual agent. The paper therefore qualifies the claimed architecture rather than validating its exact progression.

entry.title: Scholarly Growth Separated Review Audit Reputation Qualification
entry.summary: Trovò and Massari provide a concrete but partial analogue for the claimed institutional assembly. Ants-Review separates issuers, peer reviewers, approvers, and community contributors; stores the paper and each submitted review on IPFS with hashes recorded on Ethereum; keeps reviewer recommendations and author replies permanently accessible; and lets an approver accept a review and set its reward according to assessed quality. The authors also treat review work as a source of community reputation and propose community voting over review quality. This supports the feasibility of separating production from review while preserving an auditable record and attaching later reputational consequences. It does not, however, bind final judgment to accumulated standing, and its community-voting automation is future work rather than a demonstrated mechanism. The paper therefore qualifies the full arc

entry.title: Scholarly Growth Reputation Authority Risk Qualification
entry.summary: Manzoor, Chen, Lee, and Smith provide empirical reason to qualify the design guarantee. In a seven-year panel of more than one million online debates, they isolate a causal reputation effect after controlling for unstructured argument text: reputation increased persuasion beyond the validity, strength, and presentation of the arguments, and ten additional reputation points raised persuasion probability by 31% over the platform average. They characterize reputation as a low-effort heuristic proxy for argument quality and warn that visible participant characteristics can distort consensus toward reputed participants. This supports making reasons inspectable, but shows that reason visibility alone does not prevent standing from functioning as authority; an implementation must also constrain, segregate, or counteract reputation cues during merits evaluation. The evidence is from human online

entry.title: Scholarly Growth Truebit Computation Adjudication Qualification
entry.summary: Teutsch and Reitwießner independently instantiate the core adjudicative function in a narrower blockchain-computation setting. TrueBit invokes a verification game when a challenger disputes a solver's answer to a computational task; the parties iteratively narrow the contested execution step, and bounded judges rule whether the challenge is justified. The procedure is task-bound and ends in a consequence-bearing determination, making it functionally analogous to a temporary adjudicative institution for machine work. This is a qualification rather than equivalence: TrueBit uses an incentive-driven solver-challenger game and the Ethereum miner community as judges, not Kaal's purpose-convened validation pool or broader agent-governance substrate.

entry.title: Scholarly Growth Recency Identity Premium Qualification
entry.summary: Vu, Zhang, and Aberer independently instantiate a narrower version of Kaal's two-ended temporal constraint. Their provider-selection protocol considers only the provider's most recent interaction and can blacklist a provider after recent cheating, so a large stock of older standing cannot indefinitely mask current behavior. Separately, a provider's pseudonym acquires an identity premium that increases with tenure; leaving and rejoining forfeits that accumulated value, making whitewashing non-optimal for a rational provider. This qualifies rather than fully validates Kaal's design: the source models a human service marketplace, uses a most-recent-rating rule rather than continuous score decay, and imposes an economic identity premium rather than Kaal's non-transferable REP and broader institutional history.

entry.title: Scholarly Growth Peer Validated Contribution Qualification
entry.summary: Olifer independently supports a narrower peer-validation form of Kaal's accrual rule. In his network-community model, members submit documents with verifiable content; three randomly selected independent reviewers decide authenticity by simple majority; and reputation increases only after the submitted document is evaluated as authentic, while a negative evaluation reduces it. That mechanism makes a community validation decision, rather than mere activity or self-assertion, the gate for reputation accrual. It qualifies rather than fully validates Kaal's design: Olifer models document-authenticity review in a bounded community, not Kaal's broader REP ledger, legal or technical institutional attestations, capability tags, stake, citation weighting, or production governance substrate.

entry.title: Scholarly Growth Domain Specific Trust Qualification
entry.summary: Casals, Fermé, and Brandão independently support the narrower domain-separation principle in Kaal's claim. Their context-aware BDI model structures information into domains and permits one agent to assign different trust or credibility degrees to the same counterpart across those domains. They illustrate the point with a doctor whose medical information deserves different credibility from the same person's sports opinions, and they warn that a global credibility degree can cause accurate domain-specific experience to be discarded. This qualifies Kaal's design choice to maintain reputation by capability domain rather than as one global score. The paper models information-sharing trust in a preliminary formal architecture; it does not implement Kaal's demonstrated-performance REP, institutional validation, or broader governance substrate.

entry.title: Scholarly Growth Citation Credit Propagation Qualification
entry.summary: Silva, Aparício, and Silva provide independent evidence for the narrower credit-propagation mechanism in Kaal's claim. Their author-ranking study distinguishes paper-level networks, which diffuse scientific credit to cited papers and then derive author credit from those papers, from author-level networks, which diffuse credit directly to cited authors. PageRank further weights a citation from an important author more heavily and updates an author's score from incoming citation links. This provides a separate AI-facing example of why a single undifferentiated reputation measure can lose material information, extending Kaal's multidimensional-reputation requirement. It does not validate the WDAG design or transfer the brand-purchase result to dataset quality.

entry.title: Streaming Towards Secure Embodied Communication Management In Ai Era Reputation Guided Age 1B16Cd7Cd4
entry.summary: Towards Secure Embodied Communication Management in AI Era reports that end-to-end encryption and Byzantine consensus impose high overhead and require global coordination, making them impractical for time-sensitive exchange among resource-constrained embedded agents. This adds an operational limit to Kaal's separate warning that cryptography alone does not answer reputation-based exploits. The abstract does not test SPoS or establish that reputation guidance resolves the attacks.
